card.hook: Picture a tree that has spent its whole life leaning away from the wind, and now poses over bright white sand like it knows you're coming. That's the fofoti tree on Eagle Beach, and guides often call it the most photographed subject on the island.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon on the map, at the southern end of Eagle Beach near Bucuti & Tara Resort. You're about 360 m south-west of the subject, so face north-east and take the short walk along the beach until the trees sit clearly against the sea.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic view of trees, sand and sea. Go 0.5x if you're close and want a whole tree plus a big sky, or try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out a single tree.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line, then keep a strip of empty sand in front so the picture has depth.
card.best_time: Aim for about 30 minutes before sunset, when the trees stand out as dark shapes against the orange sky. Sunrise is lovely too, with soft side light on the sand.
card.selfie_here: Try the wind-bent fofoti trees on the sand at the south end of the beach, next to Bucuti & Tara Resort. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and let the twisty tree curve over your shoulder. Guides disagree about which end has the 'main' tree, so a second popular one is at the north end.
card.rules_and_safety: The fofoti trees are protected: don't climb them, hang anything on them or stand on their roots, though sitting below or near them for a photo is fine. Sea turtles nest here from April to October, so keep lights away from the nests at night.
card.challenge: Catch the whole curve of one tree as a dark silhouette against the brightest part of the sky, with a strip of empty sand at the bottom. Bonus points if you stay off the roots and still look relaxed.
card.good_to_know: Eagle Beach, also called Arend Beach, is the widest beach in Aruba and has been rated one of the best in the world. The sand is soft and white, the resorts behind it are low-rise, and the beach is public, so you can walk along it freely.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the phone icon on the map, at the southern end of Eagle Beach near Bucuti & Tara Resort. You're about 360 m south-west of the subject, so face north-east and take the short walk along the beach until the trees sit clearly against the sea.

selfie_research.notes: Sources disagree on which end of Eagle Beach the main fofoti tree is on (south near Bucuti & Tara in One Happy Island; north end in TripExpert and She Saves She Travels; end of beach in front of Amsterdam Manor in an older Tripadvisor forum post), so check the location before going. No page I found states selfie stick or tripod rules for Eagle Beach; the Disney and Sea.Hear.Now rules in my results do not apply here. A separate blog says divi divi trees are protected and cannot be cut without permission, but that concerns a different tree species. The coordinates you gave sit at Eagle Beach, which pages describe as lying between Oranjestad's cruise terminal and Palm Beach, so the Oranjestad label is loose.

card.hook: Picture the far end of a pier with turquoise water in every direction, and a sailboat drifting into your shot like it was booked for the occasion. That's Palm Beach, and the colour does most of the work for you.
card.stand_here: Head to De Palm Pier, in Palm Beach about 6 km northwest of Oranjestad. Walk to the far end and face the sea. It's a quieter option than the busy hotel frontage.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the pier, the water and the sky in one go. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, more natural look. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out a sailboat or seabirds.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, then tap the sea or sky and slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour and the water stays rich.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise or sunset, when the light is softer and there are fewer people around. The pier's lines lead your eye towards the sunset.
card.selfie_here: Try the Hyatt Regency Aruba tropical flower garden, inside the resort grounds on Palm Beach. Use the front camera and pose among the flower beds, with the palms and sea showing behind you. For something more playful, the beachfront swing at The Ritz-Carlton on Palm Beach has the Caribbean Sea as a backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot along the Palm Beach shoreline boardwalk while you stand with the tall palms and turquoise sea behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Hyatt and Ritz-Carlton spots are on resort grounds, and we don't have access rules for them, so check locally. Eduardo's Beach Shack is on private business property, so you can only see it during opening hours.
card.challenge: Be patient at the end of the pier and wait for a sailboat or a bird to enter the frame, then snap it before it leaves. An empty sea doesn't count!
card.good_to_know: The name comes from a coconut plantation owned by Captain R.J. Beaujon, who named it after Palm Beach in Florida. The beach was officially registered under that name in 1960. The first hotel here, in the 1950s, was a set of bungalows on bare sand, a long way from today's towers.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to De Palm Pier, in Palm Beach about 6 km northwest of Oranjestad. Walk to the far end and face the sea. It's a quieter option than the busy hotel frontage.

The Ritz-Carlton swing is named inconsistently: one page calls it 'The Ritz-Carlton Swing' and another 'the beachfront swing at The Ritz', and one page pairs it with butterfly-garden text that appears to describe a different site (The Butterfly Farm, which is also described as near Palm Beach). The Palm Beach Pier is widely recommended for sunset views, but no page describes a visitor-with-landmark pose there, so I left it out.

card.hook: From a distance, Druif Beach is a long, calm stripe: sand at the bottom, water in the middle and a big sky on top. It's about as easy a picture as you'll find, so you can relax and enjoy it.
card.stand_here: Stand about 450 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here the beach is a distant feature, so think of this as your scene-setting shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole scene. If the beach looks tiny, tap 2x (or up to 5x, depending on your phone). Once you're on the sand, switch to 0.5x to fit in the full sweep of the shore.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level, because on a long flat view a tilted horizon is the first thing people notice.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light than midday. Late in the afternoon the sun is behind you when you look east from the phone icon, which lights the scene evenly.
card.selfie_here: Try the I Heart Aruba sign in the Druif Beach area. Guides call it a popular photo stop, and one says the view is better because the ocean sits behind the sign. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit low so the sign sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On the sand in front of the Tamarijn hotel, you could ask someone to shoot toward Eagle Beach while you pose; check the framing on screen before they hand it back.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site or local signs before you go in case any access rules apply to the beach.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the horizon is dead level and the shoreline sits on the lower third, with lots of sky above.
card.good_to_know: Druif Beach is on the coast of Oranjestad, the capital of Aruba. It's about 300 metres long, so you can walk it end to end in a few minutes. Conditions change from day to day, so take a few frames from different spots.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 450 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here the beach is a distant feature, so think of this as your scene-setting shot.

card.hook: This isn't a monument, and that's the fun of it: your best shot here is a field of spiky green aloe with a working factory sitting right behind it. One picture, whole story: the crop, then the place that turns it into products.
card.stand_here: Stand on Pitastraat, on the stretch beside the store and Cornelis Eman's original aloe field (Pitastraat 115, Hato). Face the field so the factory buildings sit behind the plants, and check on the spot that they line up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the wide shot of the field with the factory behind it. Then try 2x for a tighter shot of the plants with the buildings softly in the background. If you're close to the shopfront, zoom 0.5x fits the whole frontage and the aloe sign.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the aloe plants on the lower line and the factory roofline along the upper one, then crouch a little so the plants look bigger.
card.best_time: Early morning, before the heat, is the usual advice for visiting fields. It's a general tip, not a rule for this spot.
card.selfie_here: Take it in the aloe field right outside the factory, with the building behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low, and zoom 0.5x if your phone has it so the plants and the building both fit.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear closed-toe shoes if you walk the fields, because aloe leaves have serrated edges that can scratch bare legs. Access can vary, so look for the field edge next to the museum, ask staff if you're not sure, and check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the one plant that looks like it's posing, tap it, and use portrait mode so the factory goes soft behind it.
card.good_to_know: Royal Aruba Aloe was founded in 1890 by Cornelis Eman and is still owned by the Eman family. The store beside the field opened in 2000, next to Eman's original aloe field, and the company received a Royal Predicate in 2021. The museum offers tours in English, Dutch, Spanish and Papiamento, so you can see parts of the production process.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Pitastraat, on the stretch beside the store and Cornelis Eman's original aloe field (Pitastraat 115, Hato). Face the field so the factory buildings sit behind the plants, and check on the spot that they line up.

selfie_research.notes: The landmark is the Royal Aruba Aloe factory, museum and store at Pitastraat 115 in Hato, Oranjestad; the coordinates you gave match that address. Only one selfie spot was supported by the pages I found. No page names a vantage point for a passer-by to photograph the whole building, so I left that field empty rather than guess. Sources disagree on access: Atlas Obscura says guests can walk the fields outside the factory, while WonderfulMuseums says the tour only gives a clear view and you may not walk among the plants much. Look for the field edge next to the museum on arrival. No page mentions selfie stick or tripod rules. Photography is generally allowed in the fields and museum, but one guide says some areas may be restricted, so ask staff.

card.hook: Hotel towers on one side, a pond full of cormorants on the other: Bubali Bird Sanctuary is a wild little wetland that somehow sits right beside the hotel strip. It's all flat water and green reeds, so the birds are the stars.
card.stand_here: Climb the wooden observation tower on the north side of the wetland (the phone icon on the map marks the spot), opposite the Old Dutch Windmill. Face out over the two ponds. Heads up: the sanctuary is in Noord, a short drive north of central Oranjestad, not in the town itself.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch both ponds in one wide shot. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a heron, egret or coot, because the birds look small from up here.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the waterline on the lower third, so the reeds fill the middle and the sky takes the top.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when guides say the birds are most active and the light is softer.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the observation tower deck with the wetland lagoon behind you. Use the front camera, and try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, to squeeze in more of the wetland over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the road opposite the Old Dutch Windmill, by the tower, and frame you with the tower and wetlands behind you (it's an approximate spot, so check the view when you get there).
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your flash off so you don't disturb the birds. Hornets may nest in and around the tower stairs, so keep a little distance, leave them alone, and use your judgement on the climb, since some visitors say the tower is worn.
card.challenge: Play bird bingo: get a wide shot of the whole wetland, then zoom in and catch one bird mid-wingflap or standing perfectly still. Tap it on screen before you shoot!
card.good_to_know: This 20-hectare wetland began life as a wastewater treatment facility. It's now an Important Bird Area, recognised by BirdLife International. About 24% of the area burned in September 2018.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Climb the wooden observation tower on the north side of the wetland (the phone icon on the map marks the spot), opposite the Old Dutch Windmill. Face out over the two ponds. Heads up: the sanctuary is in Noord, a short drive north of central Oranjestad, not in the town itself.

card.hook: Here's a church that doesn't hide: one clear building, a big open sky behind it, and a gentle walk through Oranjestad to reach it. Treat it like a stroll with a photo at the end.
card.stand_here: Start near Venezuelastraat, about 450 m north of the subject at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Walk towards the church and stop where you get a clear view of the front, with enough distance that you don't have to tilt the phone up.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x to fit the whole church in. If the street is narrow and you're close, try zoom 0.5x, and use zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for details like the front or the top of the building.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the church's vertical edges up with them so the walls stay straight instead of leaning in.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light than midday, because the sun is lower. Avoid taking photos during a service.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low and out to the side. Keep the church over your shoulder so it fits in the frame with you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working church, so be considerate of anyone arriving for a service. If you'd like to go inside, dress modestly and check locally first for visiting arrangements.
card.challenge: Take two shots of the church, one straight-on and one from a slight angle, then decide which is calm and which has more depth. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: St. Francis of Assisi Church was built in 1829 and is counted among the most important churches on Aruba. It's the pro-cathedral, a temporary cathedral, of the Diocese of Willemstad. Services are held in Papiamento and English.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start near Venezuelastraat, about 450 m north of the subject at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Walk towards the church and stop where you get a clear view of the front, with enough distance that you don't have to tilt the phone up.

selfie_research.notes: No selfie spot, passer-by photo spot, selfie-stick or tripod rule, or safety point was named on any page I found, so I have left these empty rather than guess. Pages that name the church locate it at J. Irausquinplein 3 in Oranjestad (Waymarking, Wikidata, Monumentenfonds Aruba), and Wikimapia lists J.E. Irausquinplein as a square (https://wikimapia.org/11282720/Juancho-E-Irausquinplein). That is a findable place but no source calls it a photo spot, so I did not use it. Doubtful items: a Tripadvisor traveler photo captioned as a labyrinth behind Saint Franciscus Church is said by a reviewer to be the Alto Vista Chapel, not this church (https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g147248-d536493-Reviews-or20-San_Francisco_di_Asis_Pro_Cathedral-Oranjestad_Aruba.html). Another Tripadvisor review describes a church on a hilltop with sea views, which does not match the downtown site, so I did not use it either. Sources checked: Monumentenfonds Aruba (https://monumentenfondsaruba.org/st-francis-church-oranjestad-1919/), Waymarking (https://www.waymarking.com/waymarks/WMXT46_Pro_Cathedral_of_St_Francis_of_Assisi_Oranjestad_Aruba), Wikidata (https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q23662587), Frommers (https://www.frommers.com/destinations/aruba/attractions/san-francisco-church/). A local search for a photo spot at the church square or along the street in front of the rectory may give better results.

card.hook: Picture a bright green streetcar rolling down a shopping street with no cars, no cables overhead and colonial-style buildings on both sides. That's Oranjestad, and it's a very easy win for your camera roll.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of Caya Betico Croes, the pedestrian shopping street in downtown Oranjestad. Face along the track so the tram rolls towards you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the tram and street. Tap 0.5x to fit in the full width of the street and the buildings on both sides, or try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) when the tram is still far away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the track on a line so it leads into the photo, with the tram a little off-centre.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day, when the light is softer and the street is likely to be quieter. Running days and hours can change, so check with Arubus before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the loop at Plaza Nicky, at the east end of Caya Betico Croes, where the tram turns full circle. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep a tram in the frame behind you. You can also try the same trick on the main street with a tram passing behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Trams share the street with walkers, so keep to the pavement, stay off the rails and stay alert. Running days and the route can change, so check before you go.
card.challenge: Catch one of the open-top double-deckers coming straight towards you, with the rails leading right to it.
card.good_to_know: This is the first and so far the only passenger rail service on Aruba and in the Dutch Caribbean. It was inaugurated on 22 December 2012, and regular service started on 19 February 2013. The cars run on batteries and hydrogen fuel cells, so there are no overhead wires and you get a clean line of sky above the tram.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the middle of Caya Betico Croes, the pedestrian shopping street in downtown Oranjestad. Face along the track so the tram rolls towards you.

card.hook: This isn't a jaw-dropping-view kind of stop. It's a 'prove you were here' stop, and that's a perfectly good reason to pull out your phone. A plain frontage with the name on it makes a neat souvenir of your Oranjestad wander.
card.stand_here: Stand at the National Archaeological Museum Aruba itself, because the phone icon on the map is right at the museum. Face the building and walk back as far as is practical to fit the whole frontage in.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the building as you see it. If you can't step back far enough, tap 0.5x to squeeze it all in, and use 2x for a closer shot of a doorway or sign without walking into the road.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line them up with the edges of the building so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows than midday. Weekdays may be quieter, but check the museum's own times first.
card.selfie_here: Use your front camera, switch to 0.5x if it's available, and hold the phone a little low so the museum's name sign sits over your shoulder. Take a few, because the building is wide and it likes to sneak out of the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside a museum is often limited, so check the official site before you go. Entry may be ticketed or restricted too.
card.challenge: Get the museum's name and straight walls in one shot, with not a single stranger walking through the frame.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in 1981 as the Archaeological Museum of Aruba. In 2009 it moved to a new location and took its present name. Its collections run from about 2500 BCE to the 19th century, and you may spot the Papiamento name, Museo Arqueologico Nacional Aruba, on signs.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the National Archaeological Museum Aruba itself, because the phone icon on the map is right at the museum. Face the building and walk back as far as is practical to fit the whole frontage in.

selfie_research.notes: No fetched page names a spot where a visitor stands with the National Archaeological Museum Aruba behind them, so I did not add one. The closest matches are general: airial.travel says the historic building and its artifacts 'offer great photo opportunities' without naming a place to stand (https://airial.travel/attractions/aruba/oranjestad/national-archaeological-museum-aruba-iqGKyje3). The museum sits at Schelpstraat 42, and VisitAruba says it is two streets behind Royal Plaza (https://www.visitaruba.com/national-archaeological-museum-of-aruba/). The nearby 'I Love Aruba' sign at Lloyd G. Smith Blvd 19 is a popular photo spot (https://www.kupi.com/en/explore/aruba/oranjestad/i-love-aruba-sign), but no page places it with the museum in the background, so I left it out. A Wikimedia Commons photo of the museum gives only GPS coordinates for its camera position, not a named place, so I could not use it for the passer-by spot (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Archaeological_Museum_Panorama_(1),_Oranjestad,_ARUBA.JPG). No page I found mentions selfie-stick or tripod rules or a safety point for this site. Museum pages do say flash may be restricted inside (https://airial.travel/attractions/aruba/oranjestad/national-archaeological-museum-aruba-iqGKyje3), but that is not a selfie-stick or tripod rule, so I did not list it. A field check of the street frontage on Schelpstraat, or a search for a specific photo spot on that street, would be the next step.

card.hook: Most buildings in town are shiny and new, but this one has been standing since the 1700s, and it's got the thick, plain walls to prove it. Those clean shapes against Aruba's bright blue sky practically photograph themselves.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon near Oranjestraat, about 35 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east. From here the whole fort sits in front of you, so you can frame it without moving much.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole fort in one frame. If it won't fit from where you're standing, tap 0.5x, and use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the walls up with the vertical lines so nothing leans, then tap the fort and drag the slider a touch darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows on the walls. Midday sun in Aruba can be harsh, so nudge the picture darker if you're here then.
card.selfie_here: Head to the base of the Willem III Tower and stand beside the two original cannons, so the tower rises up behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold it a little low and tilt up so the tower fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the Fort Zoutman courtyard and frame you with the fort's walls and architecture filling the background behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The fort houses a museum, so going inside may be ticketed or restricted. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the spot where two walls meet and make it the star of a shot, with the lines perfectly straight (gridlines are your friend).
card.good_to_know: Fort Zoutman dates from the 18th and 19th centuries, so this is the real thing, not a modern copy. It now houses the Historical Museum of Aruba, which explains the history of the island and its people in both rural and urban areas. The Fundacion Museo Arubano (the Aruban Museum Foundation) has run it since 1992.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon near Oranjestraat, about 35 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east. From here the whole fort sits in front of you, so you can frame it without moving much.

selfie_spots.detail: stand by the two historic cannons at the foot of the tower so the tower rises behind you
selfie_spots.why: The tower is the fort's most recognizable feature, and the cannons add a historic prop in the foreground.

card.hook: Some spots make you hunt for the angle. This one doesn't. The Parliament of Aruba in Oranjestad shows you its whole front from a short walk back, so you can relax and just take the photo.
card.stand_here: Stand near Oranjestraat at the phone icon, about 50 m south-east of the building. Face north-west and you'll have the whole front in view without tilting your phone up.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for one wide shot of the building and what's around it. Then zoom 2x or more (5x if your phone has it) for the entrance and the details. If people or traffic push you closer, 0.5x will still fit it all in.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line up the roof and wall edges with them, so the walls stay nice and straight.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to a building front than harsh midday sun. Check which way the front faces, because the light looks different from each side.
card.selfie_here: Try Plaza Henny Eman, on the eastern corner of the government complex, beside the statue of Henny Eman. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the building over your shoulder. This is our best guess for a shared frame, so check the angle on site.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the sidewalk on L.G. Smith Boulevard (number 72) to face the front of the Parliament, while you stand in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working government building, so stay on public ground, be considerate of staff and visitors, and follow any signs. If you want to go inside or take photos there, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one close-up of the entrance, then pick the one with the fewest cars and passers-by wandering through.
card.good_to_know: The Parliament of Aruba is in Oranjestad and is the building shown on this map spot. It's a working government building, but you can photograph it from the outside. Standing a little to one side makes it look more three-dimensional than straight on.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Oranjestraat at the phone icon, about 50 m south-east of the building. Face north-west and you'll have the whole front in view without tilting your phone up.

selfie_spots.why: It is the only named spot a page places right next to the Parliament, so the statue and building could share a frame, though no page says this is the best angle.

card.hook: Picture a harbour where horses once waited to board ships bound for Jamaica. That's how Paardenbaai, the Bay of Horses, got its name, and today it's where ships pull up alongside the quay and people stream on and off.
card.stand_here: Walk down to the harbour front in Oranjestad (about 3 minutes on foot from the centre) and stand about 190 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face north-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole harbour and any big ship. Switch to 1x for a natural view, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one ship or detail across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and sit the horizon on one line so the sea stays level, with a strip of quayside or railing in the foreground.
card.best_time: Any time works, since the harbour is open day and night. Go when a ship is alongside, because ships plus people on the quay make the liveliest picture.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with a story, go to the Rosalinda blue horse sculpture at the corner of Lloyd G. Smith Blvd and Werfstraat. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and tuck the horse in beside or behind you. Fancy a second one? Ambrosio, the only male of the blue horses, stands next to Casa Tua Barcelona Restaurant in downtown Oranjestad. Note that the horses are the backdrop here, not the harbour.
card.ask_someone: At the Rosalinda corner of Lloyd G. Smith Blvd and Werfstraat, hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to take you standing beside the horse.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working passenger port, so some areas may be restricted. Follow any signs and staff instructions about where you can walk and take photos, and check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get a ship's hull, a strip of quay and a bit of sky all in one frame, with the horizon sitting right on a gridline.
card.good_to_know: The harbour has been in use since 1796, and nearby Fort Zoutman dates from the same year. Oranjestad grew up around it. Cargo moved to Barcadera, and Paardenbaai has been passengers-only since 2016. Part of the port now sits in the Taratata area, on land reclaimed in the 1920s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk down to the harbour front in Oranjestad (about 3 minutes on foot from the centre) and stand about 190 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face north-east.

selfie_spots.why: She is one of eight life-size blue horse sculptures from the Paardenbaai art project, so the horse ties the photo to the harbor's history.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a viewpoint with the harbor or bay directly behind the visitor, so both selfie spots are the blue horse sculptures from the Paardenbaai art project, not the harbor itself. The landmark coordinates match the Paardenbaai Wikipedia entry (12.51980, -70.04225), which describes it as the main passenger seaport of Aruba. The Waymarking pages date from 2019 and the sculptures may have moved. The Ambrosio page gives an address at Aventura Mall, Oranjestad, while the Rosalinda corner is given as a street intersection. The ask-someone standing position is not stated by any source; it is only the same corner. No page stated selfie stick or tripod rules, and no page gave a safety point about this site.

card.hook: Here's a fun Oranjestad surprise: the "Protestant Church" is really two churches standing side by side, and everyone uses the one name for both. Pale walls, a tall tower and a clear blue sky make it an easy, happy photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Wilhelminastraat, on the pavement in front of number 1, with the church just to the north. Face the church and look up at the tower and facade.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x. If you're close and the tower won't fit, tap 0.5x. Save zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for details like the 1846 ironwork on the older building's portico.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't look like it's leaning, then tap the facade and slide it a little darker to keep the sky deep blue and the white walls crisp.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day so the sky behind the tower is properly blue. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the walls.
card.selfie_here: Use the pavement on Wilhelminastraat in front of the church entrance (number 1), since that's the church's main face. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the tower over your shoulder with some open sky above.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the street below the church, looking up at the tower, while you stand on the pavement in front of the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is usually locked, so plan on photographing from the street. If you hope to go inside or visit the Bible Museum, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one photo of the big 1950 church, then walk a few steps and find the year 1846 in the ironwork. Can you tell which building is which in your gallery later?
card.good_to_know: The larger church was inaugurated on 28 May 1950 and designed by C.M. Bakker. Next to it, the old church from 1846 is the second oldest surviving building in Oranjestad after Fort Zoutman, and its tower was added in 1867. The old church was restored in 1988 and now serves as an exhibition and concert hall, and it houses the A. van den Doel Bible Museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Wilhelminastraat, on the pavement in front of number 1, with the church just to the north. Face the church and look up at the tower and facade.

selfie_spots.name: Wilhelminastraat sidewalk in front of the church entrance
selfie_spots.detail: On the pavement of Wilhelminastraat, facing the church front (Wilhelminastraat 1). No page names an exact vantage point, so this is an inference from the street address.
selfie_spots.why: Reviewers say the building photographs well against open blue sky, and the front is the main face of the church.

The selfie spot and passer-by spot above are inferred from the Wilhelminastraat 1 address and reviews that suggest photographing from outside or below. Do not confuse the two churches: the larger Protestant Church (consecrated 1950) stands at the corner with the older Old Protestant Church (1845-46), which sits a few steps to the west; the historical marker on Wilhelminastraat refers to the older building. Reviews report the church is usually locked and used only for special occasions, so photographs are taken from outside. Your position (12.51943, -70.03650) matches the church's listed coordinates. No pages I found mention selfie stick or tripod rules.

card.hook: This is a museum about coins where you can't spend a single minute inside, because it's closed. That makes it a quick, honest photo stop on your walk around Oranjestad.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, because it marks the former Numismatic Museum itself. There's no walk and no direction to face. Just look around for the building and step back if there's room to fit it all in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole frontage. If the street is too narrow to fit it all in, drop to 0.5x. Go to 2x for close frames of lettering, doors or windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the walls and roofline with them so the building stands up straight.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the shadows are gentler. Midday sun is harsher and can wash out the sky.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x so more of the building fits in, and stand with the frontage over your shoulder. Take a few frames and check that the signage or doors are still visible behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum is closed, so don't plan on going in. Shoot from the public street, and be tactful if the building is in private use. Keep an eye on passing traffic and people while you line up your shot.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole frontage, then find one small detail, like lettering, a door or a window, and make it the star of a second photo.
card.good_to_know: The Numismatic Museum of Aruba (Museo Numismatico Aruba in Papiamento) was founded by J. Mario Odor and opened on 13 November 1981. Its collections covered coins, paper money and stamps from Aruba and other countries. It's now closed, but it's still a small piece of Oranjestad's cultural history.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, because it marks the former Numismatic Museum itself. There's no walk and no direction to face. Just look around for the building and step back if there's room to fit it all in.

selfie_research.notes: No selfie spot or passer-by spot with the Numismatic Museum of Aruba as the backdrop is named on any page I found, so I have not listed one. The main problem is that the museum appears to be closed. Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numismatic_Museum_of_Aruba) calls it a former museum that is now closed. Tripadvisor (https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g147248-d147633-Reviews-Numismatic_Museum-Oranjestad_Aruba.html) lists it as permanently closed, and recent reviews say the building is empty with a lease sign. Addresses also conflict: Wikipedia gives Weststraat 15 ('The Yellow House'), while other pages give Zijstraat 7 or Zuidstraat 7 next to St. Francis Church. Your coordinates (12.52090, -70.03980) are close to the Wikipedia coordinates. Before sending anyone, confirm with a current source that the museum is closed or has moved. The Aruba photo guides I found name spots near downtown (for example the I Love Aruba sign and the wooden swing on Plaza Daniel Leo), but none of them mention this museum, so I did not use them. No rules about selfie sticks or tripods and no safety point were stated on any page I found.

card.hook: Everyone lines up for the lime-green front of the Stadhuis, but the side wall is where the building shows off. Coral stone, carved balconies and a tile-lined sidewalk, and hardly anyone in your shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on the block between Wilhelminastraat and Caya G.F. Betico Croes, out on the pavement. Face along the side wall so the street leads your eye toward the facade.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the side wall and facade together. If the pavement is too narrow to fit it all in, drop to 0.5x. Then try 2x to pick out the balcony carvings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the side wall up with one of them, then tap the wall and drag the brightness slider a touch darker so the light stone doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning. The low light brings out the texture in the stone, the balcony carvings and the tiles.
card.selfie_here: Try the fountain in Plaza Padu, just behind the administration building. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the colonial-style buildings fit in behind you. Don't count on City Hall showing up in the background from there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the street on the Wilhelminastraat side, far enough back to fit the whole green-and-white building in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: City Hall sits right next to a busy street, so watch the traffic when you step back. It's also used for weddings, so be considerate around the entrance. Photos of couples or the doorway may be restricted, so keep your shots to the architecture.
card.challenge: Find three different textures in one frame: stone, carving and tile. Bonus points if you can get all three without a single person in it.
card.good_to_know: City Hall is also called the Eloy Arends House. Doctor Jacobo Eloy Maria Arends had it built as a home for his bride, and they married in 1925. The architect was Chibi Wever, and the design drew on South American Neo-Baroque. Today it handles civil registration, passports and weddings, and it was restored in 1997 and again in 2014.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the block between Wilhelminastraat and Caya G.F. Betico Croes, out on the pavement. Face along the side wall so the street leads your eye toward the facade.
